notes: Homelessness and EEA immigration interaction; Gage J's refusal of JR and costs split are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Homeless EEA spouse: council may rely on Home Office immigration refusal
key_facts: Mrs Burns, a Nigerian national, was evicted from Southwark accommodation in March 2004 and sought homelessness assistance.
Southwark found her homeless but ineligible under section 185 because she had no recourse to public funds and her immigration status was undetermined.
She argued she was entitled to remain as the spouse of an Irish EEA national and that the council should exercise discretion under section 188(3) to accommodate her pending review.
The council refused interim accommodation, relying on the Home Office's refusal of a residence permit under the Immigration (EEA) Regulations 2000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a local authority's refusal to provide interim accommodation under section 188(3) pending a section 202 review.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the council's decision was not irrational in relying on the Secretary of State's refusal of a residence permit rather than making its own immigration assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a residence permit has been refused by the Secretary of State, a local housing authority may reasonably rely on that decision when exercising its discretion under section 188(3) not to provide interim accommodation, even where the applicant claims EEA family-member rights; immigration status is primarily a matter for the Home Office.
legal_issues: Whether Southwark acted unlawfully in refusing section 188(3) accommodation pending review
Whether the council was required to make its own assessment of EEA residence rights
Whether reliance on the Home Office refusal fettered discretion or frustrated Community rights
Costs where legal aid funding was uncertain
linked_authorities: R v Camden LBC ex p Mohammed [1998] 30 HLR 315
R v Wandsworth LBC ex p O [2000] 1 WLR 2539
Baumbast v Secretary of State for the Home Department (Case C-413/99) [2002] 3 CMLR 23

confidence.notes: Core housing and immigration interaction and outcome are explicit. Costs and permission-to-appeal discussion is ancillary.

notes: Planning inspector reasons challenge on visibility splays and junction spacing; quashing and discretion analysis are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Planning inspector quashed for failing to decide visibility splay dispute
key_facts: Mr Ashton challenged a Secretary of State inspector's decision allowing demolition of a bungalow and construction of seven apartments at Mount Road, Tettenhall Wood.
Objectors argued the inspector failed to address disputed highway safety issues on visibility splays (X distance 2.4m vs 4.5m) and junction spacing.
Expert evidence conflicted on whether DB32 or Places, Streets and Movement governed the appropriate X distance.
The inspector addressed Y distance but adopted 2.4 metres for X distance without explaining rejection of the 4.5 metre case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application to quash a planning appeal decision for failure to deal with material considerations and inadequate reasons.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed; leave to appeal refused. First Secretary of State ordered to pay claimant's costs subject to a 15% reduction for an abandoned ground.
enrichment.ratio: Where visibility splays and junction spacing were principal controversial highway safety issues at inquiry, the inspector was required to engage with the dispute over the X distance and explain his reasoning; failure to do so was an error of law, and discretion to refuse relief was not made out.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector failed to take into account material considerations on visibility splays
Whether adequate reasons were given for preferring a 2.4m X distance
Whether junction spacing and vehicle hooking risks were ignored
Whether relief should be refused in the exercise of discretion
linked_authorities: Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council v Secretary of State for the Environment [1990] 61 P&CR 343
South Bucks District Council v Porter [2004] UKHL 33
Simplex GE (Holdings) Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment [1988] 3 PLR 25

confidence.notes: Grounds, highway guidance, and quashing order are clearly stated.

notes: Clifton brownfield/open space appeal; Sullivan J's refusal of PPG3 and PPG17 challenges is well reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Clifton residential appeal upheld despite loss of informal open space
key_facts: Bristol City Council challenged an inspector's grant of planning permission for 9-10 dwellings on a derelict L-shaped site at Cumberland Place and Granby Hill, Clifton.
The site had been used informally by residents after wartime demolition but was fenced off and subject to a pending Town Green application.
The council refused permission citing loss of open space under Local Plan policy NE1 and unacceptable design.
The inspector held the site was previously developed brownfield land with no current amenity value and that lack of a PPG17 paragraph 10 assessment was not fatal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to a planning inspector's decision allowing residential appeals A and B.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the inspector's approach to PPG3 Annex C and PPG17 was not unreasonable.
enrichment.ratio: Whether a previously developed urban site remains open space for planning purposes involves planning judgment on the particular facts; here the inspector could rationally treat the intensely urban site as brownfield, conclude amenity use was unlikely to revive, and reject the council's criticism of the absence of a formal PPG17 surplus assessment.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector misapplied PPG3 Annex C on previously-developed land
Whether the site had blended into natural surroundings in an urban area
Whether PPG17 paragraph 10 required a formal open space assessment
Whether fencing the site could circumvent open space protection

confidence.notes: Inspector's reasoning and both grounds of challenge are fully addressed. Design ground was not pursued.

notes: Standing, late service, and PPG6 retail challenge on Hanley regeneration scheme; Blackburne J's summary judgment analysis is comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Commercial developer lacks standing to challenge Hanley retail permission
key_facts: Lear Management obtained called-in planning permission for a large mixed retail and leisure scheme at Hanley, Stoke-on-Trent.
Morbaine Ltd, a Widnes developer negotiating over a rival Helical site, issued a section 288 challenge after learning of the decision.
Local resident Ms Roberts was paid £1,000 by Morbaine under a collaboration agreement to bring parallel proceedings.
Lear applied to strike out or enter summary judgment, arguing Morbaine was not an aggrieved person, service was late, and the grounds had no merit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Strike-out and summary judgment applications in linked section 288 planning challenges.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment entered against both claimants; Morbaine lacked standing, service was out of time without excuse, and the PPG6 grounds had no real prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: Commercial opportunism by a stranger developer seeking to protect a rival scheme does not make a claimant an aggrieved person under section 288; a resident funded and controlled by such a developer may amount to an abuse of process, and late service will not be excused where the grounds are meritless.
legal_issues: Who is an aggrieved person under section 288
Whether Ms Roberts' funded claim was an abuse of process
Whether late service of the claims should be overlooked
Whether PPG6 employment, sequential test and regeneration policies were misapplied
linked_authorities: R (Kides) v South Cambridgeshire DC [2003] JPL 431
Lardner v Renfrewshire Council [1997] SLT 1027
Bolton MBC v SSE ex p Greater Manchester Waste Disposal Authority (1990) 61 P&CR 343

notes: Attorney General's unduly lenient sentence reference; DTO uplift and individual mitigation are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient community orders replaced with detention for canal assault
key_facts: Three teenage offenders pleaded guilty to causing grievous bodily harm with intent after a sustained attack on a 14-year-old boy.
They stole his bicycle, beat him, threatened to kill him, broke his arm and threw him into a canal in Dame Street, London.
The recorder sentenced Stechman and Griffin to community punishment and rehabilitation orders with curfews; Walton received a community rehabilitation order.
The Attorney General referred the sentences as unduly lenient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 on the ground that community sentences were unduly lenient.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; Stechman and Griffin sentenced to 24-month detention and training orders, Walton to a 12-month DTO reflecting seven months already served in custody.
enrichment.ratio: Deliberate serious violence by groups against a child victim ordinarily requires custody; although youth and mitigation matter, community orders here failed to reflect the gravity of unprovoked group violence culminating in attempted drowning.
legal_issues: Whether the community sentences were unduly lenient
Appropriate sentence for section 18 GBH with intent by young offenders
Effect of double jeopardy and time already served on the substituted sentence
Whether different treatment of Walton was justified
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference No 59 of 1996 [1997] 2 Cr App R (S) 250
Attorney General's Reference Nos 30 and 31 of 1998 [1999] 1 Cr App R (S) 200
Attorney General's Reference No 121 of 2002 [2003] EWCA Crim 684

notes: Destination of appeals ruling in lease forfeiture case; Tanfern and Lloyd Jones applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: County court strike-out appeal in forfeiture claim goes to High Court

statutes_considered.title: Access to Justice Act 1999 (Destination of Appeals) Order 2000

key_facts: Scribes West, a former leaseholder/chargee, sought relief from forfeiture after Relsa Barkers peaceably re-entered Barkers Centre premises and granted a new lease to Settle Up.
County court proceedings involved competing strike-out and summary judgment applications on whether RB could forfeit without registered reversion.
Judge Mayer struck out the claim and substituted RB for RA as first defendant, without making a final declaration binding all interested parties.
The parties disputed whether appeal lay to the Court of Appeal as a final decision on a multi-track Part 7 claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory ruling on the destination of appeal from a county court order dismissing amendment and striking out a claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal held to lie to a High Court judge, not the Court of Appeal; Part 55 claims commenced on Form N5A are Part 7 claims for Destination Order purposes.
enrichment.ratio: A strike-out or summary judgment order is not a final decision under the Destination Order because it would not finally determine the proceedings whichever way it was decided; the destination of appeal must be ascertained from the order actually made, not from what might have been decided on a preliminary issue.
legal_issues: Whether Judge Mayer's order was a final decision under Article 1(2)(c)
Whether a preliminary issue decision on forfeiture would have been final
Whether Part 55 relief-from-forfeiture claims are Part 7 claims
Whether leapfrog to the Court of Appeal was appropriate
linked_authorities: Tanfern Ltd v Cameron-Macdonald [2001] 1 WLR 1311
Lloyd Jones v T-Mobile Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 1162
Clark v Perks [2001] 1 WLR 17

confidence.notes: Jurisdictional ruling is the sole subject matter. Underlying forfeiture merits were not finally decided.

notes: Major Bruton/Qazi secure tenancy and Article 8 judgment; court's collective conclusions at end are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Bruton sub-tenants not secure tenants of head landlord after lease termination
key_facts: Occupants of Lambeth-owned properties let through London & Quadrant Housing Trust claimed secure tenancies after Bruton v LQHT.
Lambeth terminated head-leases using break clauses, seeking possession against occupants it said had become trespassers.
The county court held the occupants were not secure tenants of Lambeth and struck out their Article 8 and Article 1 Protocol defences.
The occupants argued LQHT acted as Lambeth's agent and that human rights required a proportionality review before possession.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against county court preliminary rulings and strike-out of human rights defences in possession claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; occupants held not secure tenants of Lambeth and human rights defences struck out following Qazi.
enrichment.ratio: LQHT was not Lambeth's agent in granting Bruton tenancies; when an intermediate landlord's tenancy ends, sub-occupiers do not acquire or retain secure tenancies against the head landlord under Part IV, and Article 8 does not require a proportionality review where domestic law has already determined the occupier is a trespasser.
legal_issues: Whether LQHT granted Bruton tenancies as agent for Lambeth
Whether secure status survived termination of the head-lease
Whether Article 8 ECHR required a balancing exercise before possession
Whether Article 1 Protocol conferred additional property rights
linked_authorities: Bruton v London & Quadrant Housing Trust [2000] 1 AC 406
Qazi v Harrow LBC [2003] 3 WLR 792
Basingstoke & Deane BC v Paice (1995) 27 HLR 433

confidence.notes: Long judgment but issues and dispositive conclusions on agency, secure tenancy and ECHR are explicit.

notes: Formula One board jurisdiction dispute; Lewison J's Brussels/Lugano analysis is detailed and conclusive.

enrichment.short_title: English courts have exclusive jurisdiction over F1 director appointments
key_facts: Speed Investments challenged Bambino's appointment of the Argands as B-directors of English company Formula One Holdings.
Parallel proceedings were commenced in Switzerland by Bambino one day before Swiss service of the English claim on the Argands.
The defendants argued English courts lacked jurisdiction or should stay in favour of Switzerland under lis pendens rules.
The claim sought declarations on director identity, register rectification and validity of board resolutions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 11 application disputing jurisdiction over company director and register claims involving Jersey and Swiss defendants.
enrichment.outcome: Jurisdiction challenges dismissed; Articles 22/16 conferred exclusive jurisdiction on English courts despite Swiss proceedings being first seised as to the Argands.
enrichment.ratio: Proceedings concerning the composition of a company's board and rectification of its register of directors fall within the exclusive jurisdiction provisions for company constitution and public registers; where the English court has Article 16/22 exclusive jurisdiction, it may proceed even if second seised under Article 21.
legal_issues: Whether director appointment disputes are within Article 22(2)/Article 16(2)
Whether register rectification falls within Article 22(3)/Article 16(3)
Whether the claim was merely contractual rather than constitutional
Whether lis pendens required a stay in favour of Switzerland
linked_authorities: Grupo Torras SA v Al-Sabah [1996] 1 Lloyd's Rep 7
Ashurst v Pollard [2001] Ch 595
Canada Trust Co v Stoltzenberg (No 2) [2002] 1 AC 1

confidence.notes: Jurisdiction analysis is thorough. Underlying merits of director dispute were not decided.

notes: Police disciplinary board sex discrimination immunity; split reasoning but dismissal outcome is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial immunity bars sex discrimination claim over police disciplinary hearing
key_facts: Miss Heath, a civilian police station reception officer, complained that a Metropolitan Police inspector sexually assaulted her.
After a police disciplinary hearing before an all-male board, she brought an employment tribunal claim alleging sex discrimination in the board's conduct.
She said she felt intimidated by the all-male panel and was humiliated when cross-examined to demonstrate the alleged assault.
The tribunal held it had no jurisdiction because absolute judicial immunity protected the board members' quasi-judicial conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal upholding lack of jurisdiction on preliminary immunity grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the employment tribunal had no jurisdiction because absolute judicial immunity protected the disciplinary board's conduct.
enrichment.ratio: Members of a police disciplinary board conducting quasi-judicial proceedings are protected by absolute judicial immunity from suit, including claims of sex discrimination under the 1975 Act relating to their conduct of the hearing; composition of the board alone did not survive as a freestanding complaint once conduct-based claims were excluded.
legal_issues: Whether police disciplinary proceedings are judicial or quasi-judicial
Whether absolute judicial immunity extends to sex discrimination claims
Whether EU and ECHR anti-discrimination law displaces common law immunity
Whether an all-male board composition was a separate ground of complaint

confidence.notes: Immunity issue and dismissal are clear though the court divided on whether board composition alone could found a claim.

notes: Premature IAT remission in Algerian asylum appeal; Keith J's Surendran/credibility analysis is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: IAT wrongly remitted asylum appeal before deciding merits
key_facts: Mr Bouattoura, an Algerian asylum seeker, succeeded before an adjudicator on refugee and Articles 3 and 8 grounds after GIA persecution.
The Secretary of State appealed to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal, which formed a preliminary view to remit for rehearing.
The tribunal reopened credibility despite it not being in the grounds of appeal, relying on generic refusal-letter points.
The tribunal remitted before hearing submissions on the pleaded grounds relating to risk, protection and relocation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision remitting an asylum appeal for rehearing by a different adjudicator.
enrichment.outcome: Remission quashed; the tribunal must hear the Secretary of State's appeal on its merits unless permission is granted to amend on the generic credibility points.
enrichment.ratio: A tribunal should not remit an asylum appeal for rehearing, especially on credibility, before hearing the grounds of appeal; where credibility was not in the grounds and only generic refusal points were relied on, the tribunal should have decided the remaining factual issues itself unless further findings were truly necessary.
legal_issues: When an IAT may remit rather than determine an appeal itself
Whether the tribunal could reopen credibility outside the grounds of appeal
Application of the Surendran guidelines where the Secretary of State was unrepresented below
Whether relocation and protection issues required remission
linked_authorities: MNM v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2000] INLR 576
Manzeke v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1997] Imm AR 524

confidence.notes: Procedural error and relief ordered are clearly explained. Underlying asylum merits were not re-decided.
